facts.raw_span: A 31-year-old male nursing student
history of axillary hyperhidrosis
excessive sweating of the buttocks, most severe at the intergluteal cleft and sacrum
previously treated his axillary condition successfully with 20% aluminum chloride
treatment of the intergluteal cleft and sacrum with aluminum chloride was unsuccessful
used absorbent pads yet continued to soak through his pants
consequently unable to attend work
Minor starch-iodine test was performed
Areas of significant sweating were identified in the sacral region (10 × 3-cm area) and intergluteal cleft (6 × 8-cm area)
a 10 × 3-cm grid was drawn on the sacrum and a 6 × 8-cm grid was drawn on the intergluteal cleft
with the outermost dots omitted

concepts.why: The patient has a history of axillary hyperhidrosis and is now experiencing excessive sweating of the buttocks, most severe at the intergluteal cleft and sacrum.
The patient's excessive sweating is not attributed to any underlying medical condition, suggesting primary hyperhidrosis.
The patient is experiencing excessive sweating in multiple areas of the body, including the axillae and buttocks.
The patient's excessive sweating is localized to specific areas, including the intergluteal cleft and sacrum.
The patient has a history of axillary hyperhidrosis, which was successfully treated with 20% aluminum chloride.
Although not explicitly mentioned, gustatory hyperhidrosis is a possible cause of excessive sweating in response to certain foods or drinks.
The patient's excessive sweating may be triggered by emotional stimuli, such as stress or anxiety.
Although not mentioned, certain medications can cause hyperhidrosis as a side effect.
The patient's inability to attend work due to excessive sweating may be contributing to anxiety or stress.
It explains the excessive sweating of the buttocks, most severe at the intergluteal cleft and sacrum.

rationales.F02: History of axillary hyperhidrosis increases the likelihood of primary hyperhidrosis.
rationales.F03: Excessive sweating of the buttocks is a strong indicator of hyperhidrosis.
rationales.F04: Successful treatment of axillary hyperhidrosis with aluminum chloride reduces the likelihood of generalized hyperhidrosis.
rationales.F05: Unsuccessful treatment of intergluteal cleft and sacrum with aluminum chloride increases the likelihood of focal hyperhidrosis.
rationales.F09: Identification of significant sweating areas in the sacral region and intergluteal cleft is a strong indicator of hyperhidrosis.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's excessive sweating is localized to specific areas (intergluteal cleft and sacrum), which is consistent with Focal Hyperhidrosis. The Minor starch-iodine test also identified areas of significant sweating in these regions, supporting this diagnosis.
